# The Header {#sec-header}

`inspect` is not a closure you can open in the editor. It is a C entry,
`do_inspect`, living in `src/main/inspect.c` and reached through
`.Internal`. The thing being printed is a node on the heap. The line you
get back is the node's header, translated into a dialect that rewards a
little memorization.

A typical line from a length-one integer inside a classed list:

```text
19 VECSXP g0c1 [OBJ,MARK,REF(15),ATT] (len=1, tl=0)
```

Read it left to right.

| Piece | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| address | Where this node sits. Identity, for this process, right now. |
| `19` | The `SEXPTYPE` number. 19 is `VECSXP`. |
| `VECSXP` | The type name. |
| `g0c1` | Generation bit, then allocation class. |
| `[...]` | Header flags that happened to be set. |
| `(len=, tl=)` | Vector length and the allocator's true length, when the node is a vector. |

The manual's version of this layout is
[R Internals, section 1.1](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-ints.html#SEXPs).
The header changed shape in R 3.5.0. Older blog posts that describe a
32-bit `sxpinfo` are describing a previous machine.

## The type tag is five bits

`SEXPTYPE` occupies the first five bits, so there is room for 32 tags.
[The table in the manual](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-ints.html#SEXPTYPEs)
is the one to trust. The ones a session like this actually meets:

| Code | Name | At R level |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | `NILSXP` | `NULL`, and only `NULL` |
| 1 | `SYMSXP` | names |
| 2 | `LISTSXP` | pairlists: attributes, formals |
| 3 | `CLOSXP` | ordinary functions |
| 4 | `ENVSXP` | environments |
| 5 | `PROMSXP` | promises |
| 6 | `LANGSXP` | calls |
| 7 | `SPECIALSXP` | specials: `[`, `{`, `if`, `function` |
| 8 | `BUILTINSXP` | builtins: `sum`, `+`, `c` |
| 9 | `CHARSXP` | a single cached string, inside a character vector |
| 10 | `LGLSXP` | logical |
| 13 | `INTSXP` | integer |
| 14 | `REALSXP` | double |
| 15 | `CPLXSXP` | complex |
| 16 | `STRSXP` | character |
| 17 | `DOTSXP` | `...` |
| 19 | `VECSXP` | list |
| 21 | `BCODESXP` | byte code |
| 22 | `EXTPTRSXP` | external pointer |
| 23 | `WEAKREFSXP` | weak reference |
| 24 | `RAWSXP` | raw |
| 25 | `OBJSXP` | S4, and S7 instances |

Codes 11 and 12 are a genuine piece of archaeology, not a rumor. The manual
says they were used for internal factors and ordered factors, and were
withdrawn. The numbers survive in serialized objects, so the gap cannot be
casually reused. Factors today are integers with attributes. That story is
in @sec-in-context. `OBJSXP` used to be spelled `S4SXP`; the comment is
still sitting in `sexptype2char`.

There is also a pseudo-type `FUNSXP` with code 99, used in a few internal
tables to mean "some kind of function." You will not see it in an inspect
line. `ANYSXP` (18) is a placeholder for "any argument," and there are no
objects of that type.

## `g0c1` is two different fields

The generation and the class are neighbors in the printout and unrelated
in the header.

`gcgen` is one bit. Inspect prints it as `g0` or `g1`. It will never print
`g2`. The collector itself is richer than the bit: `memory.c` keeps a
nursery plus old generations (`NUM_OLD_GENERATIONS` is 2, and the comment
next to it says the header bit is why you cannot have more than that).
What you can actually see is the bit. In a live session, freshly allocated
nodes tend to show `g0`. The nodes that have been around since startup ---
`R_NilValue`, locked symbols, cached `CHARSXP`s --- show `g1`. Treat `g1`
as "this has survived, or was born old." Treat a blog post that decodes
`g0c1` as "generation 0 of 3, size class 1 of a vague scale" as out of
date.

`gccls` is three bits, so eight allocation classes. The manual's
[allocation-class section](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-ints.html#Allocation-classes)
and the comment in `memory.c` agree:

| Class | What lives there |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Non-vector nodes, and the zero-size bucket |
| 1--5 | Small vectors, with room for 8, 16, 32, 64, and 128 bytes |
| 6 | Custom allocators (`allocVector3`), not counted as ordinary R memory |
| 7 | Large vectors, `malloc`'d individually |

That is the whole of "random access versus cons" as a memory-manager
question, and it is not stack versus heap. A pairlist node is class 0
because it is not a vector. A length-one integer is class 1 because four
payload bytes fit in the 8-byte bucket. A length-one character vector is
also class 1: one pointer. An environment's hash table of a few dozen
slots is class 7: twenty-nine pointers do not fit in 128 bytes. Empty
`character()` and empty `integer()` landed in class 0 in the dumps,
because a zero-length vector has nothing to put in a data page.

Small vectors come out of pages of about 2000 bytes. Large ones are their
own allocations. Custom-allocator vectors can share memory in ways R's
accounting refuses to pretend to understand. ALTREP, later, is a further
escape hatch: the node can exist before the data does.

## The flags are the header talking

The bracket is a selection, not a full register dump. The fields live in
the 64-bit `sxpinfo` structure quoted in the manual:

```c
SEXPTYPE type      :  5;
unsigned int scalar:  1;
unsigned int obj   :  1;  /* class attribute? */
unsigned int alt   :  1;  /* ALTREP? */
unsigned int gp    : 16;
unsigned int mark  :  1;
unsigned int debug :  1;
unsigned int trace :  1;
unsigned int spare :  1;
unsigned int gcgen :  1;
unsigned int gccls :  3;
unsigned int named : 16;  /* the reference count, these days */
```

The flags worth knowing by sight:

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `OBJ` | The `obj` bit. This is what `is.object()` answers. A class attribute sets it. |
| `ATT` | The attribute pointer is not Nil. Attributes are a pairlist. |
| `MARK` | The collector has marked the node in this collection. |
| `REF(n)` | The reference count. |
| `LCK` | Locked. Common on symbols and on locked bindings or environments. |
| `gp=0x…` | Sixteen general-purpose bits. Their meaning depends on the type. |
| `ALT` | Not always spelled that way in the bracket, but the `alt` bit is how ALTREP is recognized. |
| `GL` | Shows up on the global environment in inspect output. |

`gp` is where people get inventive, and it is worth resisting. On a
`CHARSXP` the inspect line often already translates the bits you care
about: `[ASCII] [cached]`, sometimes with `ATT` because the character
cache hangs information off the attribute pointer. The manual has a
section on
[CHARSXP encodings](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-ints.html#Encodings-for-CHARSXPs)
and another on the
[cache](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-ints.html#The-CHARSXPs-cache).
Symbol `gp` values (`0x4000`, `0x6000`, `0x7000`, `0x8000` in the dumps)
are a different code book. They are decoded in the source, not in a stable
user manual, and this book leaves them on the
[open list](open-questions.qmd) rather than inventing a table.

## `REF(65535)` is a saturated count

`NAMED_BITS` is 16. Under the reference-counting build,
`REFCNTMAX` is `(1 << 16) - 1`, which is 65535. `MARK_NOT_MUTABLE` sets
the count to that ceiling. Incrementing past the ceiling is a no-op, and
decrementing a saturated count is also a no-op: the macros in `Defn.h`
refuse to move a count that has hit the cap. A saturated node stays
saturated. That is the technical meaning of **immortal** in these notes.
The collector is not invited to free it, and the copy-on-modify logic is
not invited to mutate it.

`R_NilValue` is constructed that way on purpose. So are a lot of other
process-lifetime nodes: many symbols, `R_TrueValue`, `R_FalseValue`, the
canonical logical `NA`. A high count on a value you just created is a
different phenomenon. It means something in the process is holding the
node. The evaluator, the protection stack, `.Last.value`, a promise, an
attribute, an environment binding, and an IDE's object browser all count.
The same binding can print `REF(1)` in a quiet console and a much larger
number under RStudio, because RStudio is a holder. The count is a census
of current pointers. It is not a property of the source literal.

A fresh empty vector in those dumps printed an empty bracket, `[]`. A node
with a positive count printed `REF(n)`. Read a missing `REF` as "no
tracked holders worth printing," and then go look at `inspect.c` before
you build a theory on the absence. The field still exists.

## Where `inspect` sits

The symbol `inspect` in the internal table is a `SYMSXP` whose internal
pointer aims at that C routine. You do not hold the printer as a value in
the way you hold the vector you asked it to describe. `.Internal` and
`.Primitive` are the subject of
[chapter 2 of the same manual](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-ints.html#Internal-vs-_002ePrimitive).
Primitives are the fast path. Internals are the slightly more ordinary
one. Neither is "an R function that happens to be written in C" in the way
a `.Call` wrapper is. They are entries in the interpreter's own table.

One more ambiguity the manual states cleanly, because the dumps make it
easy to miss: an environment is both a frame and an enclosure. The frame
is the bindings. The enclosure is the parent you walk when a name is
missing. Hash tables, when present, are a `VECSXP` of pairlists, and the
empty buckets are the Nil singleton, over and over, at one address. That
picture is the whole of the next two chapters.
